stories.title: Anthropic's first day on Nasdaq: opened 34% above its IPO price, then gave back half and closed at $97.17, up 17%
stories.label: HOT
stories.window: Today to Sun 22 Nov: the first-day story is news until Monday's trade; after that it becomes a stock-price story (no price levels or charts under the SEBI rule).
happening: Anthropic (Nasdaq: ANT) priced its IPO at $83 and began trading just after 11:30 am ET on Thu 19 Nov at $111.50, a 34% premium (Yahoo Finance live blog).
It rose as high as $115.10, then fell through the afternoon and closed at $97.17, up 17% from the IPO price (Yahoo Finance; Forbes and Bloomberg headlines say the same).
After 30 minutes it was about 13% below its opening trade; SpaceX was up almost 10% at the same point in its June debut (Yahoo Finance).
Its opening pop of 34% was about three times SpaceX's 11%. About $15 billion of stock changed hands in the first minute, nearly twice SpaceX's ~$9 billion (Yahoo Finance).
It raised $81.3 billion selling 980 million shares, the largest IPO raise on record (Yahoo Finance; CNBC 18 Nov).
Ashton Kutcher's A-Grade put in $435 million early; that stake is now worth roughly $7 billion (Yahoo Finance, citing Newsweek).
curiosity_gaps: People who bought at the open lost about 13% by the close, while people who got IPO shares made 17%. Who were the buyers at $111.50?
It was the biggest IPO ever and it opened three times stronger than SpaceX, so why did half the pop vanish by the evening?
E15 said it was 'a share you could never buy'. Now anyone can buy it, so what did day one look like for the people who did?

stories.lane: Hot lane (new: CAG draft audit of BIS reported 17 Nov; the week's biggest money topic on Indian Reels)
stories.title: Hallmark on your gold, but who checked it? A CAG draft audit says BIS skipped 43.7% of its required checks on hallmarking centres, and inspected 5,444 of 28,865 jewellers in 2024-25
stories.label: HOT
stories.window: Through the wedding season, about two weeks; the next turn is the Consumer Affairs Ministry's reply or the report reaching Parliament.
happening: A CAG draft audit report on the Bureau of Indian Standards found BIS carried out 2,826 of the 5,020 prescribed surveillance audits of Assaying and Hallmarking Centres (the labs that test purity before the hallmark goes on) from 2020-21 to 2024-25: 2,194 missed, a 43.7% shortfall (Business Today, 17 Nov, citing The Hindu BusinessLine).
Worst regions: Kolkata did 359 of 1,345 (73.3% short); Delhi 348 of 1,063 (67.3% short); Chandigarh missed 38.8%; Chennai 14.45% (Business Today).

In 2024-25 BIS inspected 5,444 of 28,865 licensed jewellers, leaving 23,421 unchecked that year; over the five years more than 83% of registered jewellers missed their annual inspection (APAC News Network, 17 Nov).

BIS blamed manpower shortages and the difficulty of collecting samples in remote areas; the CAG called that inadequate. The draft has gone to the Consumer Affairs Ministry and goes to Parliament after that (APAC News Network).
Separately, a Dainik Bhaskar sting on rhenium-mixed gold getting a 22K hallmark is driving most of the views; we could not open the original report, so its numbers are unverified.
curiosity_gaps: Every jeweller says 'hallmark hai'. The audit says the people meant to check the hallmark labs skipped 2,194 checks. So who is checking?
4 out of 5 licensed jewellers were not inspected in a year, and the regulator's answer is 'we're short of staff'.
It's wedding season. Is the 22K you're paying for actually 22K?

stories.others_takeaway: Everyone made the rhenium sting and 'check the HUID'. Nobody told it from the audit's own numbers: 2,194 missed checks, 4 in 5 jewellers unchecked, and the regulator's 'staff shortage' reply. The joke lands on the system.

facts.text: 2,826 of 5,020 prescribed AHC surveillance audits done, 2020-21 to 2024-25; 2,194 missed; 43.7% shortfall; Kolkata 359/1,345 (73.3%), Delhi 348/1,063 (67.3%), Chandigarh 38.8%, Chennai 14.45%; draft audit report.

2024-25: 5,444 of 28,865 licensed jewellers inspected, 23,421 not; over 83% missed annual inspections over five years; ~2.3 lakh registered jewellery establishments; BIS cited manpower and logistics, CAG found it inadequate; draft sent to the Consumer Affairs Ministry.

watch_out: It is a draft audit: say 'CAG's draft report', not 'CAG proved fake gold'. Missed inspections are not proof that hallmarks are fake.

The rhenium-sting numbers (1 g rhenium in 7.83 g gold, 22K916 hallmark) appear only in creators' descriptions; we could not open the Bhaskar original. Keep them out unless Akhilesh wants them, and then source them first.
'5,444 of 28,865' is one year (2024-25); '83%' is the five-year figure. Don't mix them.

Gold has been in the outliers for weeks; this is a consumer-protection story, not a gold-price call. Bets: B4 (gold close-up and '2,194 checks missed' on the top half), B3 (a line a viewer sends to whoever is buying wedding gold).

stories.lane: Deep lane (The Ken, 19 Nov: 'The costlier mutual fund plan is still called regular, and most investors are in it'; facts from open pages)
stories.title: Direct plans became the default on fund-house websites on 1 November, yet 70% of retail and HNI mutual fund money still sits in the costlier 'regular' plans
stories.label: COLD
stories.window: Evergreen, but it rides on the 1 November SEBI change; best within two weeks while 'direct default' is new.
happening: From 1 November, SEBI made direct plans the default option on fund houses' own websites and apps; regular plans stay, and existing investments don't move by themselves (The Ken subhead; Business Today and 5paisa explainers).
Even so, 70% of retail and HNI mutual fund assets are still in regular plans (The Ken, 19 Nov, public subhead).
Regular plans cost more because the expense ratio includes a distributor's trail commission, paid every year for as long as the money stays invested (Business Today, 13 Nov).

Business Today's illustration: a Rs 10,000 monthly SIP for 20 years, assuming 12% a year in direct and 11% in regular, ends at Rs 98.9 lakh vs Rs 87.4 lakh, a gap of Rs 11.5 lakh. These are assumptions, not returns (13 Nov).
curiosity_gaps: The cheaper plan is now the default button, and 70% of the money still sits in the expensive one. Why?
It's called 'regular', which sounds normal. It's the one that pays a commission every year, forever.
One percentage point a year sounds small. On a Rs 10,000 SIP over 20 years, assumed returns put the gap at about Rs 11.5 lakh.

Rs 10,000 monthly SIP, 20 years, 12% (direct) vs 11% (regular) assumed: Rs 98.9 lakh vs Rs 87.4 lakh, gap Rs 11.5 lakh; invested Rs 24 lakh each; illustrative, not guaranteed.

watch_out: The 70% is The Ken's figure for retail and HNI assets; older AMFI/CRISIL data puts the direct share of individual investors' AUM at about 30% (Mint), which agrees. Credit 'via The Ken' in the caption.
Any return in the example is said as an assumption ('12% maan ke'). No 'switch now' or fund names: it is about plan type, not a buy/sell call.
Distributors do give advice; aim the joke at the label and the lifetime trail, not at people who chose regular.
